::: {.why}
There is no such thing as a ten-year price history for a contract that expires quarterly, so every futures backtest starts with a construction choice that changes the answer.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Name three ways to splice a continuous series and say what each does to the return series and to the price level.
- Show that a naive price-splice creates returns that nobody could have earned.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Build all three from whatever contract data or ETF proxies you have: an unadjusted price splice, a back-adjusted series where the gap at each roll is subtracted from history, and a ratio-adjusted series. Plot the three and note that the back-adjusted one can go negative far enough back, which is a real property and not a bug.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Show the error: compute the return series from the naive splice and find the fictitious return on each roll date, then report the annualised size of that artifact. This is the single most common futures backtest mistake and it can be worth several percent a year.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Fix the convention in qlib: returns come from within-contract price changes, never across a roll, and the continuous series exists only for display. Write it as a docstring rule and a test.
:::
:::

:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Futures are in contango and you roll. What happens to a long position's return, and why is losing money on the roll not the right description?
:::
